The paper introduces Trans-EnV, a framework for evaluating the linguistic robustness of large language models (LLMs) against English varieties. The framework automatically transforms Standard American English datasets into 38 English varieties (18 dialects and 20 ESL variants) by combining expert-curated linguistic rules with LLM-based transformations. Evaluations across six benchmark datasets and seven state-of-the-art LLMs show substantial performance disparities. 

Comprehensively, this paper makes a timely, high-impact contribution by introducing the first scalable framework to systematically evaluate LLMs on diverse English varieties. Despite some initial concerns about task scope and validation rigor, the authors addressed them thoroughly during rebuttal with additional experiments and clarifications. The combination of expert-driven methodology, extensive empirical evidence, and community resources ensures strong scientific merit and long-term value. We believe this work directly advances fairness and robustness in LLM evaluation, making it suitable for acceptance at NeurIPS 2025.

author_final_remarks.value:
We sincerely thank the reviewers, ACs, and SACs for the time and effort they dedicated to our work. This process has been a valuable opportunity for us to engage in meaningful and constructive discussions. To aid in the final decision, we briefly summarize our contributions and the outcomes of the discussion.

Our work introduces **Trans-Env**, a framework that automatically transforms Standard American English (SAE) datasets into multiple English varieties to evaluate the robustness of large language models (LLMs) to linguistic variation. The framework is grounded in expert-curated linguistic resources, and its construction was validated through rigorous statistical testing and consultation with a linguist, ensuring linguistic validity. Through extensive experiments with seven LLMs across six benchmarks, we demonstrate that LLM performance is impacted by linguistic changes.

The main initial concern in the reviews was that our experiments were limited to closed-ended tasks. To address this, we conducted additional experiments on open-ended tasks across three datasets (IfEval, AlpacaFARM, and MT-Bench) with four models on eight dialects and ten ESL variants. These results confirm that LLMs still exhibit degraded performance compared to SAE, underscoring the necessity of our transformation framework. Furthermore, during the rebuttal period, we made our best effort to address all concerns by conducting additional validations with two native speakers and providing further clarifications and analyses.

We are pleased that most concerns raised by the reviewers have been addressed, as reflected in their comments: *“They have resolved most of my concerns” (Reviewer e6nB)*, *“My initial concern was addressed accordingly, the authors’ clarification and plan for revision sound valid,” and “W2-1 was addressed by the authors’ additional experiments” (Reviewer E6DB)*. We are also grateful for the recognition of our efforts during the discussion period, with remarks noting that *“the authors’ attitude toward this submission is very impressive (thoughtful, active, and professional).” (Reviewer E6DB)* 

We deeply appreciate the opportunity to present and discuss our work, and we thank the reviewers and chairs once again for their thoughtful engagement and valuable feedback.

First of all, **I want to express my sincere APOLOGY** for making the authors feel anxious and stressed due to my ambiguous wording and bad communication. As an author of another submitted paper, I am also undergoing the same phase with the authors (doing tons of experiments with billion-scale LLM in a very limited time), so I deeply sympathize with the authors and how they feel pressured and stressed.
* **All of my concerns, except the t-test part, were addressed already through the initial response from the authors.**
* **But I just needed clarification on the details behind the t-test** (this was one of the most suspicious parts for me) before reconsidering my rating on this paper, because I have not seen any existing works that use the t-test for feature extraction/identification, if there are many papers on this approach, sorry for my lack of professionality.
* After reading the authors' faithful explanation on the t-test, my understanding of the procedure was improved, and I feel **the concern `W2-2` is also somewhat addressed**.
* Therefore, **I will raise my rating from 3 to 4** after finishing this writing!

---

Meanwhile, allow me to clarify my statement about `W3`-- "_However, as the original manuscript did not have those details, I should not change any rating regarding this_".
* I did not mean that I will not change my rating on this paper on this sentence. 
* I was just wanting to remind the fact that details lacking in the original draft, which are explained through this rebuttal thread, should not be assumed to have been originally included in the manuscript.
* I don't think the reviewer should solely judge the modification of rating based on the authors' promise to add details such as "[DESCRIPTION ON DETAILS]. We will add these details in the revised version".
* In contrast to the verbal commitment and promise on adding missing details, showing supporting evidence through additional empirical validation can change reviewers' opinion justifiably, because that evidence explicitly refutes reviewers' initial concern, even though it also did not appear in the original draft. The `W1` and `W2-1` are laid in this category.
* Moreover, for the `W2-2`, I needed clarification on how they use the t-test to precisely judge my rating, and the authors give sufficient clarification that fills my knowledge gap on that part, which can be a justification behind my reconsideration of the rating. 

---

In conclusion, 
* I am deeply sorry about bordering the authors mentally (and also physically?). For the next review, I will be more professional in terms of communication by removing any aggressive sentences that would make the author nervous and being more specific. Thanks for giving me this lesson, and sorry again for your potential mental damage.
* Departing from it, I truly enjoyed reading and reviewing this paper, which I believe has huge potential to contribute robust and reliable LLM evaluation in a distinctive manner. So, good luck!

---
FYI, This year's NeurIPS system does not allow authors to access the updated rating and final justification upon the notification date, so maybe you still see the old rating (3), but I just changed it to 4 with a valid final justification.

rebuttal.value:
**Q. Vocabulary Threshold**
Thank you for your suggestion. We conducted additional experiments using TruthfulQA with LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct. Due to time constraints, we were unable to evaluate all ESL variants. The results are presented below:

|     | A_arabic | A_italian | B_arabic | B_italian |
|-----|----------|-----------|----------|-----------|
| 15% (Reported in the paper) |     63.2 |      65.3 |       63 |      66.8 |
|  25% |     63.8 |      66.8 |     65.3 |      67.4 |
| 5% |     60.4 |      63.2 |     62.1 |      64.2 |

The 15% threshold was used in the main paper. As shown in the table, a stricter threshold (5%) leads to a decline in performance, whereas a more lenient threshold (25%) results in improved performance across all variants. We hypothesize that a stricter threshold compels the model to replace a greater number of vocabulary items with simpler alternatives, thereby increasing the degree of transformation from the original sentence and potentially compromising meaning or coherence.

We thank you for your insightful feedback and will include this analysis in the final version of the paper.


**Q. choice of LLaMA-3.3-70B as semantic checker**
When using Gemma-2-27B-Instruct as the feature transformation model, we observed instances where portions of the original questions were omitted in the transformed outputs. For example, given the original question “A man stands in an elevator as it begins to ascend. Does the normal force from the floor do work on the man?”, the initial transformed version was “The, like, normal force from the floor do work on the man?”, which omits key contextual information. In such cases, LLaMA-3.3-70B, serving as the semantic consistency checker, successfully identified the semantic misalignment.

Upon regenerating these cases, approximately 78% of the outputs retained the original meaning more accurately. summary.value: This paper introduces Trans-EnV, an automated framework that transforms Standard American English (SAE) datasets into various English varieties to evaluate the linguistic robustness of LLMs. The framework combines linguistic expert knowledge from curated resources (eWAVE database, English Grammar Profile, and ESL learner corpora) with LLM-based transformations to create evaluation datasets across 38 English varieties (18 dialects and 20 ESL English varieties). The authors transform six benchmark QA datasets and evaluate seven state-of-the-art LLMs, revealing performance drops of up to 12.5% for dialects and 46.3% for ESL English varieties compared to SAE.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The paper tackles a important fairness issue in NLP - the performance disparity of LLMs on non-standard English varieties, which affects global users who do not speak SAE.
2. Trans-EnV is built on solid linguistic foundations, utilizing expert-curated resources like eWAVE (compiled by 84 professional linguists) and the English Grammar Profile. The framework was developed in consultation with a researcher specializing in second language acquisition, ensuring linguistic validity.
3. The framework combines the scalability of LLMs with the accuracy of expert-curated linguistic features, addressing limitations of purely manual or purely LLM-based approaches.
4. The paper presents thorough experiments across 38 varieties, 6 benchmark datasets, and 7 sota models, providing compelling evidence of the robustness issues. The human evaluation (88% validity rate) and semantic checker validation demonstrate the quality of transformations.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The evaluation is restricted to QA tasks only. The generalizability to other important NLP tasks like generation, summarization, or dialogue remains unexplored, limiting the scope of conclusions about overall LLM robustness.
2. While the framework was validated by a second language acquisition researcher, there's limited validation from native speakers of the target varieties (only Spanish and French were mentioned). This could affect the authenticity of transformations.

additional_feedback.value: It would be helpful if the paper could mention the computational requirements for transformation, especially when scaling to larger datasets or stronger models.

summary.value: This paper introduces Trans-EnV, a novel and scalable framework for evaluating the linguistic robustness of Large Language Models (LLMs) against a wide array of English varieties. The authors identify a critical gap in current LLM evaluation, which is predominantly focused on Standard American English (SAE), leading to fairness and robustness concerns.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The paper tackles a crucial and increasingly relevant problem of fairness and robustness in LLMs as they become globally deployed. Creating a systematic and scalable benchmark for English varieties is a high-impact contribution for the NLP and ML communities.

2. The core strength of Trans-EnV lies in its rigorous methodology. Instead of relying on naive prompting for style transfer, it grounds the transformation process in expert-curated linguistic databases. This "expert-in-the-loop" approach, where linguistic knowledge guides LLM-driven execution, ensures the generated data is linguistically plausible and valid, a feature often missing in prior work. 

3. The experimental setup is extensive, covering 38 varieties, 6 diverse tasks (knowledge-based and reasoning), and 7 modern LLMs.

limitations_weaknesses.value: The quality of the generated datasets is inherently tied to the capabilities of the chosen feature transformer (Gemma-2-27B) and semantic checker (LLaMA-3.3-70B). A brief discussion in the limitations section about the framework's sensitivity to this choice and how the quality might degrade with less capable models would be beneficial.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value:
1. For the ESL English generation, a 15% threshold for higher-level vocabulary was used to simulate realistic proficiency. This is well-justified by analyzing a CEFR-labeled corpus. Did you perform any sensitivity analysis on this hyperparameter? How would a stricter (e.g., 5%) or more lenient (e.g., 25%) threshold affect model performance?

2. The choice of LLaMA-3.3-70B as the semantic checker is interesting. How much did this checker contribute to the final quality?

summary.value: This paper proposes the first framework that converts benchmark datasets written in standard English into diverse non-standard English variants in terms of dialects and ESL English varieties by leveraging LLM sentence transformers, guided by expert-confirmed transformation guidelines. The authors observed performance gaps between standard English and non-standard English variants, especially in ESL English varieties.

strengths_contributions.value:
* [`S1`] This work **focuses on a crucial yet (relatively) unexplored topic**, non-standard English performance analysis, in the era of LLMs. 
  * The resulting datasets and the proposed framework, Trans-Env, can be flexibly leveraged to investigate the linguistic robustness of frontier-level language models and potentially contribute to making them safer.
* [`S2`] The authors proposed a solid framework that is **scalable** with LLM-based automatic transformations, while **supporting converted sentences' validity** via expert-driven transformation guidance rules and a semantic checker model.
  * This gentle incorporation of domain expertise and model-based automation results in a scalable and reliable pipeline to be adopted in real-world scenarios.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
* [`W1`] **Limited scope of validation**
  - `W1-1`) Although the author provided demonstrations on six NLP datasets, all of them are traditional closed-form tasks that have a ground-truth discrete answer per query. 
    - However, research communities may be (much more) interested in the results on open-ended setups with human preference evaluation, such as [1,2,3], rather than closed-ended answers to reflect complex real-world use cases and be suitable for agentic-LLM evaluation. 
  - `W1-2`) Besides, given that the transformations are conducted at the sentence level, the length of sentences would be an important factor that affects the distributional discrepancy between the original and converted. Adding an analysis on the performance gap at varying average sentence lengths would deepen the insights from this benchmarking setup.
* [`W2`] **Lack of rigor in statistical tests and their significance**
  - `W2-1`) In Figure 2, the author claims correlations between the performance gaps and linguistic distances between the two datasets. However, the author did not provide any actual value, e.g., correlation coefficients from some statistical tests and corresponding p-values, and claimed the correlation based on just scatter plot (or barplot) visualizations, where the tendencies are unclear enough.
    - Explicit correlation analysis between performance gap and linguistic distance [4] should be accompanied to justify the statement.
  - `W2-2`) Meanwhile, in line 153-154, the author said they identified distinct features that are attributed to varying native language-proficiency levels via t-test. 
    - However, the t-test is a statistical test that scrutinizes the mean difference between two groups [5], rather than identifying explanatory variables that affect the variance of the response variable. That is, t-test does not tell the individual features' importance to the variance of the response variable (language proficiency). To my knowledge, Logistic Regression (and seeing fitted coefficients) or ANCOVA would be valid statistical methods for this.
    - I would appreciate it if the authors could clarify for which variables and for what purpose the t-test was applied here.
* [`W3`] **Lack of rigor in human study**
  - `W3-1`) Claiming validity based on domain experts' oversight without detailed rationales.
    - In line 120-121, line 156-157, and line 174, the authors said like "was verified by the specialist, ..., were reviewed by the researcher" without any justification on (1) _how did that expert make the verifications?_ and (2) _based on what criteria?_. 
    - Missing justification on the above important facets weakens the rigor of the proposal.
  - `W3-2`) Missing details on the recruiting process of the participant to evaluate the quality of the converted sentence.
    - Although the authors provided the instruction and actual evaluation process screenshot in the Appendix, they did not reveal the recruiting process of participants and their statistics, which makes the reliability of human evaluation results questionable due to potential selection bias [6].
  - The authors may refer to Section 2 of the GPQA paper [7], which elaborates on details about the human-in-the-loop dataset construction pipeline.

---
> Reference
1. Zheng, Lianmin, et al. "Judging llm-as-a-judge with mt-bench and chatbot arena." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (2023): 46595-46623.
2. Dubois, Yann, et al. "Alpacafarm: A simulation framework for methods that learn from human feedback." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (2023): 30039-30069.
3. Chiang, Wei-Lin, et al. "Chatbot arena: An open platform for evaluating llms by human preference." Forty-first International Conference on Machine Learning. 2024.
4. Jung, Haeji, et al. "Mitigating the Linguistic Gap with Phonemic Representations for Robust Cross-lingual Transfer." Proceedings of the Fourth Workshop on Multilingual Representation Learning (MRL 2024). 2024.
5. Mishra, Prabhaker; Singh, Uttam; Pandey, Chandra M; Mishra, Priyadarshni1; Pandey, Gaurav2. Application of Student's t-test, Analysis of Variance, and Covariance. Annals of Cardiac Anaesthesia 22(4):p 407-411, Oct–Dec 2019. | DOI: 10.4103/aca.ACA_94_19

(minor comments on presentation)
* **Figure 1: caption of Figure 1 lacks self-completeness and can be improved further.**
  * For Fig1-(a) please consider mentioning that LLM generates transformation guidelines, and for Fig1-(b), consider explaining that capital S and T are arbitrary LLMs that take [XX] as input to produce output [YY]
  * The final transformed sentence is also notated as $s$  -- the same notation with pre-tranformed sentence $s$, which decreases the rigor.
* **Table 4 and Table 5: confusing cell colorization.**
  * I think the most important thing to emphasize here is "how the linguistic variation drops the performance of LLM compared to that of the original standard English?". It would be better to pick the performance on the original dataset as a pivot of the colormap (white), and denote the relative improvement and degeneration as blue and orange, respectively. And you can drop the bold font for simplicity.
  * The current color gradation confuses the readers about the relative performance of the converted datasets (in a quick view, blue cells seem to be improvements), which weakens the inspiring findings of Tables 4 and 5.

I believe concerns from other reviewers were also professionally addressed through extensive experiments. Although this paper in its submitted form does not contain rigorous details behind the human study, I believe the strengths of this work outweigh my unresolved concern which is why I changed my rating from 3 to 4, leaning towards acceptance.

title.value: Trans-EnV: A Framework for Evaluating the Linguistic Robustness of LLMs Against English Varieties

abstract.value:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are predominantly evaluated on Standard American English (SAE), often overlooking the diversity of global English varieties.
This narrow focus may raise fairness concerns as degraded performance on non-standard varieties can lead to unequal benefits for users worldwide.
Therefore, it is critical to extensively evaluate the linguistic robustness of LLMs on multiple non-standard English varieties.
We introduce Trans-EnV, a framework that automatically transforms SAE datasets into multiple English varieties to evaluate the linguistic robustness. 
Our framework combines (1) linguistics expert knowledge to curate variety-specific features and transformation guidelines from linguistic literature and corpora, and (2) LLM-based transformations to ensure both linguistic validity and scalability.
Using Trans-EnV, we transform six benchmark datasets into 38 English varieties and evaluate seven state-of-the-art LLMs.
Our results reveal significant performance disparities, with accuracy decreasing by up to 46.3% on non-standard varieties.
These findings highlight the importance of comprehensive linguistic robustness evaluation across diverse English varieties. 
Each construction of Trans-EnV was validated through rigorous statistical testing and consultation with a researcher in the field of second language acquisition, ensuring its linguistic validity.
Our code and datasets are publicly available.
